newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania banks slam banking licence withdrawals.
newsitem.headline: Romania banks slam banking licence withdrawals.

text.p: Two Romanian private banks slammed the central bank (BNR) on Monday for withdrawing their licences, calling the move a mere administrative step which they said violated existing laws.
Dacia Felix SA and Renasterea Creditului Romanesc Credit Bank SA said they would contest the BNR's decision in court.

A statement from Dacia Felix, based in the Transylvanian city of Cluj said the "tough administrative step" contradicted rules on the special status of banks under reorganisation or legal liquidation procedures.
The BNR announced on Monday it had withdrawn the banking licences of the two banks after a "deterioration of their financial position due to big debts and low capitalisation".
It said its board's decision was in line with a banking law and with BNR rules on banking licences.

Last July, the BNR cut months-long financial support to Credit Bank and Dacia Felix, saying further aid might spark "uncontrollable inflationary pressure". It lodged files with Bucharest and Cluj courts seeking a ruling on their liquidation or reorganisation.
Not a single bank has been declared bankrupt in Romania, which now has 40 commercial banks, created with market reforms since the 1989 fall of communism.

"The National Bank of Romania cannot resort to two distinct procedures -- one legal and one administrative -- to reach the same goal, namely the reorganisation or liquidation of Dacia Felix," the Dacia Felix statement said.
Dacia Felix -- once a fast-growing bank, now struggling with bad debts and losses -- says it worked out a recovery plan but a Cluj court has yet to rule on its future.
The bank said that the BNR should have waited for a court ruling on its fate before lifting its licence.
A Bucharest court is due to decide on Credit Bank's future on May 8.
"The BNR hasn't informed us about its decision. When we get that notification, we will go to court over the withdrawal," Credit Bank manager Constantin Postole told Reuters.
"The BNR cannot be a sustitute for courts and decide to strip licences before rulings," Postole said.

The new centrist coalition government, which took office after elections last November, and the BNR plan to amend the existing banking law to boost the central bank's supervision powers and to cut a clear distinction between winding up procedures for banks and commercial companies.
